extracted.intended_audience: researchers, media historians, archivists, and entrants/organizers of media awards (Peabody-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Historical and procedural standards used by the Peabody Awards to evaluate broadcast and digital media, including the Board's ethos, merit principles, category/entry handling, and administrative judging practices. Covers examples of what the Board has rewarded and how processes (listening posts, citations, deliberations) have been implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: "excellence on its own terms" / "stories that matter"
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases the Board has used to summarize the Peabody ethos: there has never been a fixed set of criteria for what constitutes a winning program, but the Board has historically invoked ideas like 'excellence on its own terms' and 'stories that matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These phrases signal a flexible, qualitative standard: judges assess programs according to intrinsic quality and meaningfulness rather than a rigid checklist. The Board issues winner citations to articulate why a particular program met those ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories that contribute to an engaged citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Winner citations indicate the Board rewards 'stories that contribute in some way to an engaged citizenship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs that inform, engage, or strengthen public civic life are favored. Historical examples include news, public service, and educational broadcasts (e.g., Mayor LaGuardia broadcasts; early public service winners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service
rubrics_metrics.description: The Awards were created to honor public service radio programming; early categories and winners explicitly recognized 'public service' by stations of different sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries that demonstrably serve the public interest—providing consumer information, civic affairs coverage, or service to underserved communities—have historically been recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational merit / Outstanding Educational Program
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs judged outstanding in educational value (e.g., Wisconsin School of the Air’s 'Afield With Ranger Mac' won for Outstanding Educational Program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational entries are evaluated for effectiveness, exemplary practice, and potential to set an example to be widely followed; citations may note that a series 'sets an example which should be widely followed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Winner citations that explicitly state merits and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1942 the Peabody Board issues citations for each winner that describe the merits of the winning programs and explicitly state the reasons behind the Board's decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations are the mechanism for transparency and explanation: they summarize the Board's rationale (what was excellent or exemplary) and may use value-laden phrases to convey ethos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-based selection irrespective of entry category
rubrics_metrics.description: Although entrants select a category for administrative purposes, the final awards are not given based on those categories; 'the entire pool of submissions is considered, and the Board awards programs solely on merit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A winner is chosen from the whole submission pool and is 'simply a winner, not a Documentary winner or a News winner.' Category is for organization/filing, not determinative of awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of new forms, innovation, and evolving media
rubrics_metrics.description: Peabody has adapted to new media forms (first TV entries in 1948, first international entry in 1951, first website winner in 2003, streaming/digital winners since 2010s) and established the Futures of Media Award to recognize 'groundbreaking digital narratives and the technologies used to tell these stories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board values innovative storytelling and technological approaches; novel formats or platforms that advance narrative or public service may be grounds for recognition. Student Honor Board selects Futures of Media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of distinctive artistic form (medium-sensitive evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has recognized that different media may constitute distinct art forms (e.g., noting that drama on television is 'neither a stage play nor a movie, but a separate and distinct new art form').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation takes account of the medium’s particular qualities; judges should assess works in light of what the medium can uniquely achieve rather than applying inappropriate cross-medium standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of listening posts and local recommendations to broaden scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting in 1943 the Board established 'listening posts'—volunteer advisors across regions who recommend notable broadcasts and write up local programming they find worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decentralized scouting via volunteers increases the diversity of submissions considered; recommendations from listening posts feed into the entry pool and help surface local excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry documentation and judging facilitation (entry digests and forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peabody Awards Office prepared bound digests containing basic entry information (title, station call letters, location) and brief excerpts from entry descriptions; entry forms instruct entrants to select a category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardized, summarized documentation helps judges review many submissions efficiently. Entrants must provide metadata and descriptive excerpts to facilitate evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition and impartial evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A national advisory board administered jointly by NAB and UGA included 'twelve other outstanding American citizens who have demonstrated...interest in public affairs' and were 'prepared to evaluate, in an impartial and detached manner, the contributions' of stations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection panels are constituted to ensure impartiality and public-affairs expertise; membership and stature of board members are part of legitimacy and quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and procedural practices (screening committees, meeting length, entry fees, archives access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural measures implemented over time include expanding Board meetings to multiple days and moving them to UGA for access to programs, adding entry fees, expanding faculty and student screening committees, implementing standardized forms, and making archives/exhibitions available to promote awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative and logistical practices (time for deliberation, screening layers, standardized submissions, funding through fees) are treated as part of ensuring rigorous, fair evaluation and program sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of finalists and honorable mentions (variable recognition structures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has changed how many and what kinds of intermediate recognitions it announces (e.g., early honorable mentions; in 2015 Peabody announced sixty finalists of which thirty would be named winners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition structures (finalists, honorable mentions, number of winners) are flexible tools the Board uses to communicate standards and highlight work even when not all are full winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards to individuals and organizations (flexible recipient types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peabody has issued awards to Individuals and Organizations, with shifting definitions of those categories over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both individual creators and institutional producers may be eligible; evaluators consider appropriate attribution (individual vs. organization) when recognizing contributions.
